banking.summary: A bank lends money and moves money. Almost everything an auditor looks at traces back to one of those two activities, or to the obligation banks carry to know who their customers are.
hallmarks: Lending decisions bent by commercial pressure — exceptions to credit policy that become routine, and limits raised the day after an order was blocked
Security that turns out to be worth less than recorded, or was never legally registered in the first place
Customer checks treated as paperwork rather than a legal duty, with alerts closed in bulk to clear a backlog
Payments and branch cash, where money physically leaves and small repeated losses add up
Numbers built on assumptions — how much will not be repaid, how customers will behave in a crisis — that nobody independently challenges
banking.compliance: Expect obligations covering capital and liquidity, customer due diligence and financial crime reporting, expected credit loss accounting, consumer protection and complaint handling, and data protection.

insurance.summary: An insurer takes money now and promises to pay later. Its accounts therefore rest on estimates of a future nobody has seen yet, which is where most of the audit attention belongs.
hallmarks: The money set aside for future claims — an estimate large enough that a small nudge changes the reported result
Claims settled for more than the policy required, because nobody re-read the wording
Reinsurance that does not respond the way everyone assumed when the large loss finally arrives
Business written outside appetite or priced below what the risk deserves, to protect volume
Intermediaries selling in the insurer's name, whose conduct becomes the insurer's problem
insurance.compliance: Expect obligations covering solvency and capital adequacy, technical reserving and actuarial sign-off, product governance and fair treatment of customers, intermediary licensing, and claims handling standards.

logistics.summary: A logistics business moves other people's goods using vehicles, people and premises spread across a wide area. Margins are thin, so losses that look small are not.
hallmarks: Deliveries made but never invoiced, or invoiced at the wrong rate — revenue that simply disappears
Fuel, which is easy to take and hard to tie back to a specific vehicle or trip
Freight changing hands repeatedly, with each handover a chance for it to go missing or be damaged
Subcontracted carriers moving your freight without the insurance or safety record you assumed
Driver, vehicle and cross-border compliance, where a failure stops the operation rather than just costing money
logistics.compliance: Expect obligations covering driver hours and fitness to drive, vehicle roadworthiness, transport of hazardous goods, customs and trade documentation, and revenue recognition over the period of carriage.

aviation.summary: Airlines and ground handlers run expensive assets under strict safety oversight. Records are not administration here — if the paperwork is incomplete, the aircraft does not fly.
hallmarks: Maintenance that was performed but cannot be evidenced, or certified by someone whose authorisation had lapsed
Tickets sold long before the flight, so what counts as earned revenue and what is still owed to the customer needs care
Leased aircraft that must be returned in a defined condition, at a cost decided years earlier
Ground damage and delays where responsibility is disputed and often absorbed
Fuel and services billed by suppliers against volumes nobody independently verified
aviation.compliance: Expect obligations covering continuing airworthiness and maintenance certification, crew and engineer licensing, ground handling and safety management systems, dangerous goods acceptance, and lease and revenue accounting.

manufacturing.summary: A manufacturer buys materials, converts them, and holds significant stock throughout. Most of the value — and most of the risk — sits in that stock and in the accuracy of what it cost to make.
hallmarks: Costs used to value products that no longer reflect what inputs actually cost, so margins are wrong everywhere
Material that goes in but does not come out as sellable product, absorbed into variances instead of investigated
Stock that exists on the system but not on the floor, and counts performed by the people responsible for it
Product that will never sell at full price still carried at full cost
Safety and environmental conditions that must be evidenced, not merely asserted
manufacturing.compliance: Expect obligations covering workplace safety, environmental permits and emissions reporting, product safety and liability, waste handling, and inventory valuation standards.

retail.summary: Retail is a very large number of small transactions across many locations. No single one matters, which is exactly why losses accumulate without anyone noticing.
hallmarks: Refunds, voids and discounts processed against real sales, with the cash taken
Stock lost to theft, process error and short deliveries, all blended into one shrinkage figure
Money promised by suppliers counted as profit before the conditions to earn it have been met
Gift cards and loyalty points, which are money owed to customers and easy to understate
Store-level performance measured on sales, with control quietly deprioritised
retail.compliance: Expect obligations covering consumer protection and pricing accuracy, card payment security, product and food safety where relevant, employment standards, and stored-value or unclaimed balance rules.

hospitality.summary: Hotels handle cash, stock and people at every property while central oversight is stretched thin. Most losses are small, local and repeated.
hallmarks: Rooms given away, discounted or comped at the front desk with no independent approval
More food and drink consumed than sales explain, with the gap written off as waste
Purchasing done locally, at higher prices, sometimes from suppliers connected to staff
Distribution channels taking commissions large enough to erase the profit on a room
Deposits and loyalty balances held for stays that already happened, or never happened
hospitality.compliance: Expect obligations covering food safety and hygiene, licensing, card payment security, employment and service charge rules, and guest data protection.

ecommerce.summary: An online retailer is built from transactions and customer data. Money travels from the customer through a payment provider to the bank, and needs reconciling at every step.
hallmarks: Orders taken, money collected by the payment provider and cash in the bank that do not reconcile
Fraudulent orders fulfilled, with the payment reversed after the goods have gone
Refunds issued without the goods ever coming back, or to a different payment method
Prices and promotions published at scale, where an error is honoured before anyone can react
Personal data kept longer and shared wider than the basis for holding it allows
ecommerce.compliance: Expect obligations covering data protection and marketing consent, card payment security, consumer rights on cancellation and returns, distance selling disclosure, and marketplace liability where third parties sell.

fmcg.summary: Consumer goods companies sell through retailers and distributors and spend heavily on promotions to hold shelf space. That spend, and product safety, carry most of the risk.
hallmarks: Promotional money committed without anyone checking whether the promotion worked
Deductions taken by customers against invoices and settled without being verified
Stock pushed into the distribution channel near period end to meet targets, returning later
Batch traceability that has never been tested, so a recall would be slow
Short-dated stock still valued as though it will sell at full price
fmcg.compliance: Expect obligations covering food and product safety systems, labelling and advertising claims, recall and withdrawal procedures, competition rules on pricing and distribution, and trade promotion accounting.

utilities.summary: Utilities run safety-critical networks under close regulatory oversight, often with prices and service levels set externally. Compliance is not discretionary, and neither is asset safety.
hallmarks: A gap between what is delivered into the network and what is billed, filled with estimates
Licence and determination conditions nobody owns, so compliance is asserted rather than evidenced
Safety-critical maintenance deferred under cost pressure, with the risk transferred to the public
Customers in hardship or dependent on supply for health reasons, treated as ordinary arrears cases
Capital projects capitalised before the asset is actually in service
utilities.compliance: Expect obligations covering the operating licence and price controls, customer protection and vulnerability rules, network safety and environmental standards, metering accuracy, and regulatory reporting.

telecom.summary: Telecoms handle enormous transaction volumes that pass through several systems before becoming a bill. Records lost along the way are services given away free.
hallmarks: Usage recorded on the network that never reaches billing, so it is never charged
Services activated for customers who were never properly credit assessed or set up to be billed
Amounts owed by other operators settled using their figures rather than your own
Network changes made without control, where an outage becomes a reportable event
Long-lived free-of-charge, test and employee accounts with real consumption
telecom.compliance: Expect obligations covering the operating licence, service continuity and outage reporting, subscriber identity and data retention, consumer contract and billing transparency rules, and interconnect settlement terms.
